title: 1Password adds browser login feature for AI agents
content:
Give agents access without giving up your passwords
1Password will connect to your personal agents, whether you have one or multiple, so they can work without seeing your passwords. Join the waitlist to be notified when your agent is ready.
how it works
1Password for Agents keeps private information private
Step 01 - The agent asks
At the login screen, the agent asks for the credential for your account. You can allow it to connect to 1Password.
Step 02 - you decide
Approve or deny login access through 1Password. Any new account information is saved in your 1Password vault.
Step 03 - 1Password logs in
1Password autofills the password or one-time code. Your agent only sees that access is granted and doesn’t see your password.
Trusted by millions to protect how they live and work
Secure the accounts your personal agents use
Whether you have one AI agent or multiple, you’ll be able to connect 1Password to any or all supported agents. 1Password for Agents is included in all Individual and Family plans.
Muse
Rolling out over the coming days across all platforms.
SpaceXSI Grok Bot
Rolling out over the coming days across all platforms.
More agent connections, secured by 1Password
Sign up to be notified when your agent is ready
Your credentials remain encrypted
Even when you approve access to an account, your AI agents don’t see your passwords. Everything in your vault remains protected.
Frequently asked questions
Will an AI agent see my passwords?
No. 1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password. The person sees which credential it needs and why, and then chooses whether to approve the request. That approval happens on the person’s own device, confirming that the permission came from them. 1Password then fills it directly into the sign-in form instead of sending it to the agent. Once signed in, the agent continues the task while the password stays protected in 1Password.

report.summary: 1Password launched a waitlist feature that lets AI agents sign into websites without ever seeing users’ passwords.
report.background: AI agents are moving from chat windows into browsers and apps, where they need logins to complete tasks like shopping, booking, and account management. Today, users often paste passwords into agent tools, store credentials in environment variables, or hand over full session access, all of which expand the attack surface. Password managers already solve human autofill, but agent workflows need a way to delegate a login without revealing the secret. 1Password’s move reflects a broader race to build identity and permission layers for autonomous software, as OAuth and existing passwordless standards do not cover every consumer website or personal agent. The feature also arrives as vendors push “personal AI agents” that act on a user’s behalf across multiple services.
key_points: The flow is request, approve, autofill. When an agent hits a login screen, it asks 1Password for the credential; the user approves or denies on their own device; 1Password fills the password or one-time code directly. The agent learns only that access was granted.

1Password says agents identify themselves with a unique digital key. The user sees which account is requested and why, and approval happens on the user’s device, confirming the request came from them. Credentials remain encrypted in the vault and are not sent to the agent.

The feature is included in all Individual and Family plans and is positioned for one or many personal agents. 1Password is taking waitlist signups and says early agent connections, including Muse and SpaceXSI Grok Bot, are rolling out across platforms in coming days.

The security boundary is the login step, not the whole task. Once signed in, the agent continues working, so users still need to supervise what it does. The design reduces password exposure but does not by itself prevent a compromised or manipulated agent from misusing an already authorized session.
report.impact: For the AI industry, 1Password is validating a credential-delegation model: agents get scoped access and users keep secrets. That could become a template for agent identity, approval UX, and audit trails, especially as browser agents handle commerce and sensitive accounts. For developers, it means less custom secret handling but new integration work around agent identity, consent prompts, and session boundaries. For regular users, the immediate benefit is not pasting passwords into agent tools; the trade-off is approval fatigue and trusting that the agent behaves after login. The feature does not solve prompt injection, over-permissioned actions, or sites without autofill support. Adoption will depend on which agents integrate and whether users can easily review what was accessed.
report.tools: Watch 1Password for Agents and its waitlist. For open-source credential management, evaluate Bitwarden and Vaultwarden; for agent browser automation, Browser Use and Playwright are useful for testing login flows. Also follow emerging agent-identity and consent standards, since password-manager autofill is only one piece of secure agent delegation.
